question: When several ReLU neurons implement exactly the same initial predictor, can a function-invisible positive-homogeneous rescaling determine how quickly a teacher feature is learned and which duplicate neuron becomes its unique owner under ordinary Euclidean gradient training?

key_findings.claim: A conserved scale-imbalance mark supplies optimization state that the represented function omits.
key_findings.evidence: For each two-layer ReLU unit the paper rewrites raw parameters as functional coefficient q=a||w||, feature direction s=w/||w||, and mark δ=a²-||w||². The predictor depends only on q and s, while Euclidean gradient flow conserves δ. Its exact loss-dissipation identity separates coefficient reaction from directional transport, with δ reallocating mobility between them.

key_findings.claim: Opposite gauges of the same one-neuron predictor create a sharp quadratic separation in feature-specialization time that cannot be explained by changing the global learning-rate clock.
key_findings.evidence: In the one-ReLU Gaussian teacher-student ODE, both signs converge to the teacher from any positive coefficient and non-antipodal initial direction. For fixed visible initialization and marks +D and -D, the hitting times obey T_+D=Θ(D^-1 log(1/ε)) and T_-D=Θ(D log(1/ε)), hence a Θ(D²) ratio. Their visible vector fields share the same nonzero coefficient component but different direction components, so they are non-collinear. The numerical fit gives exponent 1.97.

key_findings.claim: Among any fixed number of exactly duplicated students, the location of one favorable gauge programs the feature owner and functionally prunes all other units.
key_findings.evidence: Assigning +D to one unit and -D to all other duplicates yields winner-tube entry in O_m(D^-1), post-capture loss decay at exp(-c_m D t), convergence of the selected unit to the teacher, and every redundant coefficient to zero. Redundant directions move only O_m(D^-2) after capture. Permuting the positive mark permutes the winner while the entire initial predictor remains unchanged.

key_findings.claim: The local gauge-mobility law extends to arbitrary-depth feedforward ReLU nodes, but the global ownership theorem does not.
key_findings.evidence: Scaling a hidden node's incoming affine parameters by 1/ρ and outgoing weights by ρ preserves the complete function while multiplying the instantaneous normalized incoming and outgoing direction velocities by ρ² and ρ^-2. The authors explicitly limit this to a local statement: global specialization requires residual control and the Gaussian competition basin, and normalization or parameter sharing is excluded.

key_findings.claim: Finite-time owner selection is robust on an open set, whereas asymptotic coefficient pruning beyond exact duplicates needs explicit nondegeneracy conditions.
key_findings.evidence: The certified angle basin spans 0.77 to 0.90 radians. A sufficient perturbed-initialization radius scales at least as a exp(-b m³), with a conservative large-gauge threshold no worse than A exp(B m²), and guarantees that only the positive-gauge unit enters a fixed winner set. Long-time locking for a nonsymmetric redundant dictionary additionally assumes quotient transversality, a full active redundant coefficient frame, angle separation, and a continuation margin.

key_findings.claim: Small-step full-batch gradient descent preserves the programmed winner even though the continuous-time gauge is no longer exactly conserved.
key_findings.evidence: With raw-parameter step size η=h/D, discrete iterates shadow the fast flow to O_m(h+D^-2), enter the winner tube within O(1/h) steps, contract loss geometrically, and accumulate gauge drift O_m(h/D). The post-capture redundant-direction path retains the D^-2 scaling because every Euler remainder is weighted by the vanishing task residual.

key_findings.claim: Population and finite-sample simulations reproduce the predicted complete trajectories and scaling exponents in the tractable model.
key_findings.evidence: For m=2-32 and D=8-128, capture-time slopes range from -1.0019 to -0.9951, redundant-drift slopes from -1.9991 to -1.9907, and finite-gauge approximation slopes from -1.9981 to -1.9926, all with R² above 0.9999. Across 400 empirical-flow runs at D=32, m=2-16, and N=512-8192, every run selects the programmed owner and functionally identifiable trajectory-error slopes range from -0.4482 to -0.4942, compatible with N^-1/2.

method.core_idea: Hold the complete initial ReLU function fixed while changing only its representative on a positive-homogeneous rescaling orbit, then derive how ordinary Euclidean geometry turns that hidden choice into coefficient and feature-direction mobility.
method.mechanism: Convert each two-layer unit into marked coordinates (q,s,δ), derive exact reaction-transport dynamics and loss dissipation, and close the population ODE with the Gaussian arc-cosine kernel for one ReLU teacher. Compare opposite large marks for a single unit. For multiple exact duplicates, use permutation symmetry to reduce all negative-gauge losers to one aggregate block, analyze the D-rescaled fast flow, prove entrance into an invariant winner basin and local PL contraction, then control finite-D, perturbed, finite-sample, and raw Euler dynamics. Validate the reduced, marked, raw population, and empirical systems on full trajectories.
assumptions: Inputs are isotropic Gaussian and the target is one positive-coefficient, bias-free ReLU ridge for all global specialization and ownership theorems.
Training uses population square loss and ordinary Euclidean gradient flow; the discrete extension uses small-step full-batch gradient descent with η=h/D.
Units remain in the regular chart with nonzero input weights, positive functional coefficients, and directions away from antipodal kernel singularities during the relevant phases.
The strongest global result starts from exactly duplicate visible units, with one mark +D and every other mark -D, for fixed finite multiplicity m and sufficiently large D.
The initial teacher angle lies in the certified interval [0.77,0.90] radians for the multi-unit basin theorem.
No normalization, parameter sharing, stochastic minibatches, or ordinary symmetric weight decay alters the homogeneous gauge during the main analysis.
For asymptotic locking from nonsymmetric redundant states, quotient transversality and a nondegenerate redundant coefficient frame persist.

techniques.role: Separates the function-visible coefficient and direction from the conserved scale-imbalance variable.
Decomposes loss reduction into functional-coefficient change and feature-direction motion with different gauge-controlled mobilities.
Changes only an invisible rescaling representative so timing and ownership differences cannot be attributed to the initial predictor.
Uses exact Gaussian ReLU moments to reduce population training to coefficient and alignment dynamics.
Separates favorable D^-1 transport, unfavorable D reaction/transport layers, and O(D^-2) approximation errors.
Aggregates exactly identical negative-gauge students into one redundant block while retaining multiplicity in the metric.
Combines arc-cosine sign inequalities, finite basin entry, local feature-Gram coercivity, and a PL inequality to prove global ownership.
Machine-certifies the remaining scalar kernel inequalities and an open initial-angle interval.
Downweights directions of vanishing-coefficient neurons so finite-sample errors compare identifiable functional state rather than arbitrary dead-unit angles.
Expands original-parameter gradient-descent steps, controls chart preservation and gauge drift, and transfers continuous capture to discrete training.

limitations: Author-stated: the strongest unconditional global theorem is for exactly duplicated students; the open-set extension guarantees finite-time selection but not unconditional long-time coefficient pruning.
Author-stated: nonsymmetric long-time locking requires explicit quotient-transversality, active-frame, angle, and continuation-margin assumptions to exclude functional cancellation modes.
Author-stated: all multiplicity statements hold for each fixed m; there is no infinite-width limit, and sufficient finite-gauge thresholds can grow exponentially in m².
Author-stated: the arbitrary-depth result is only an instantaneous node-mobility law, not a global feature-ownership theorem for deep networks.
Author-stated: finite-sample N^-1/2 behavior is empirical, not a sampling or propagation-of-chaos theorem.
Author-stated: the construction does not claim that large opposite-gauge disparities occur typically under standard random initialization.

Reviewer-identified: every global experiment uses the same two-dimensional, one-feature Gaussian teacher-student problem; there is no natural dataset, multiple teacher feature, deep network, or minibatch-SGD test.

Reviewer-identified: the favorable regime takes D large while shrinking the discrete learning rate as 1/D, yielding raw parameter norms separated by roughly sqrt(D) and potentially severe numerical conditioning.

Reviewer-identified: normalization, biases in the global model, weight sharing, adaptive optimizers, momentum, stochasticity, and data anisotropy can break or substantially change the exact reduction.

Reviewer-identified: symmetric weight decay exponentially erodes the mark, and an exactly gauge-equivariant optimizer removes the function-level divergence, so the phenomenon is optimizer- and regularization-specific.
failure_modes: Batch or layer normalization destroys the simple node-rescaling symmetry, invalidating the hidden-mark intervention.
Symmetric weight decay relaxes δ toward zero before the slow negative-gauge unit specializes, especially when λD is not small.
A gauge-equivariant update such as an exactly implemented path-normalized rule keeps gauge-related function trajectories identical and suppresses programmed ownership.
Multiple teacher features can make one favorable unit insufficient or create competing basins not covered by the one-ridge proof.
Small coefficients, zero input weights, sign changes, or antipodal directions can leave the regular marked chart or violate uniform kernel bounds.
Nonduplicate redundant features can cancel functionally while retaining large individual coefficients unless the active-frame condition holds.
Minibatch noise or heterogeneous marks can break exchangeability and select a different owner before deterministic gauge transport dominates.
Very large D produces highly unbalanced raw factors and may underflow one side, overflow the other, or require impractically small stable steps.
reusable_insights: A predictor is not a complete training state: function-preserving parameter representatives can encode different optimization mobilities.
When studying feature learning, separate coefficient growth from feature-direction transport; a scalar speed or global learning-rate comparison can hide distinct phase-plane paths.
Use same-function counterfactual initializations to identify causal parameterization effects without confounding initial predictions or losses.
Track dead or redundant units in functionally weighted coordinates so arbitrary directions of near-zero coefficients do not dominate trajectory comparisons.
Check whether regularization and optimizer geometry preserve, erode, or quotient out the proposed hidden state before extrapolating a gradient-flow mechanism.
Distinguish finite-time winner selection from asymptotic coefficient pruning; the latter needs identifiability conditions in overcomplete dictionaries.
Validate reductions at the level of full loss and dissipation trajectories, not only endpoint alignment.
open_questions: Under standard random initialization, what distribution of node gauges arises and how predictive is it of eventual feature ownership?
Can the ownership mechanism be observed in deep finite-width networks on natural data after controlling for initial feature quality?
How do momentum, Adam, minibatch noise, weight decay, and normalization reshape or erase reaction-transport mobility?
What replaces unique ownership when the teacher has many reusable or correlated features?
Can gauge choice be optimized to allocate interpretable features deliberately without the numerical pathologies of very large D?
Is there a practical intermediate optimizer that preserves useful transport asymmetry while remaining invariant to irrelevant scale drift?
Can finite-sample and growing-width theorems recover the observed N^-1/2 trajectory error and characterize when noise overturns gauge selection?
Which hidden-state variables beyond scale gauge are omitted by function-space descriptions of representation learning?

competitive_landscape.title: Get rich quick: exact solutions reveal how unbalanced initializations promote rapid feature learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Kunin et al. already show that conserved imbalance from layer scales and learning-rate asymmetry changes rich-versus-lazy feature learning, with exact minimal models and broader deep-network experiments. This paper sharpens the consequence at a fixed complete predictor: it derives a node-level reaction-transport split, a Θ(D²) non-clock gap, and deterministic ownership among duplicate ReLU units.

competitive_landscape.title: Path-conditioned training: a principled way to rescale ReLU neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Path-conditioned Training exploits the same function-preserving ReLU rescaling orbit to align a path-lifting kernel and accelerate optimization in practical networks. The present paper is not a conditioning algorithm; it proves that a deliberately chosen orbit representative can assign one teacher feature to one otherwise indistinguishable neuron and prune the rest in a solvable model.

competitive_landscape.title: Scale redundancy and soft gauge fixing in positively homogeneous neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Soft Gauge Fixing introduces gauge-adapted coordinates and a norm-balancing penalty that dissipates scale imbalance and expands the stable learning-rate range. This paper studies the complementary phenomenon: leaving the imbalance intact under Euclidean training causally changes feature transport and can be used to program representation allocation.

competitive_landscape.title: Intrinsic training dynamics of deep neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Marcotte et al. characterize when deep ReLU gradient flow descends to a lower-dimensional path-lifted dynamic that still depends on initialization and conservation laws. This paper supplies an explicit shallow marked state (q,s,δ) and integrates its initialization dependence into global specialization-time, selection, and pruning theorems.

novelty_assessment: Author claim: this is the first fixed-predictor demonstration that an invisible ReLU gauge creates a sharp non-clock Θ(D²) feature-specialization gap and deterministically assigns feature ownership with functional pruning, supported by an exact reaction-transport decomposition and robustness/discrete extensions. Prior work already establishes scale-gauge conservation, initialization-dependent intrinsic dynamics, rich-learning acceleration from imbalance, gauge fixing, and practical rescaling. Reviewer inference: the defensible novelty is the unusually clean causal ownership counterfactual and its complete theorem chain, especially the separation of reaction and transport and the distinction between functional and coefficient-wise pruning. The result is mathematically strong but deliberately narrow; it does not yet show that gauge-programmed ownership is common, useful, or even visible in realistic deep stochastic training.
reviewer_notes: All 45 pages were checked, including the exact marked reduction, weight-decay and gauge-equivariant controls, single-unit global bounds, multiplicity proof, certified angle interval, open-set and conditional-locking qualifications, raw Euler analysis, and complete population/finite-sample sweep tables. Competitive comparisons were verified on primary arXiv records current through 2026-08-23. Claims about arbitrary-depth networks are intentionally labeled local because the paper repeatedly makes that boundary explicit.
